excerpt: const validPath = await validatePath(dirPath); await fs.mkdir(validPath, { recursive: true });
sink: fs.mkdir(validPath, {recursive:true}) creates real directories on disk
guard: bypassable: isPathAllowed() (filesystem.ts:184-217) compares path.normalize(...).toLowerCase() forms via normalizePath() (line 134-136); a not-yet-existing path like /home/Alice/x (case-different from allowed dir /home/alice) passes the lowercase prefix check, but validatePath's walk-up logic (lines 263-286) preserves the caller's literal case for the non-existing suffix, so fs.mkdir creates a real, case-sensitive-distinct directory tree that is not actually nested inside any allowed directory.
why: path is fully caller-controlled (CreateDirectoryArgsSchema: path:string). validatePath()->isPathAllowed() makes its allow/deny decision on a lowercased copy of the path while the real fs.mkdir operates on the case-preserved resolved path; on a case-sensitive filesystem this lets the tool create a directory outside the operator-configured allowedDirectories while the guard reports the path as allowed.

sink: edited file is read/written via TextFileHandler/DocxFileHandler at the resolved path

Because edit_block edits an existing file, the case-twin bypass only works if a file with mismatched case already exists at a path whose lowercase form matches an allowed directory prefix -- a precondition that cannot be confirmed from static reading alone, so this is a real but weaker case than the write-new-file variants.

forceTerminate() (improved-process-tools.ts:661-692) only acts on pid values present in terminalManager's own session map (or virtualNodeSessions); any pid not started by start_process returns 'No active session found for PID', so it cannot terminate arbitrary system processes.
get_config takes no schema parameters; it only reads and returns the local configManager state, so there is no caller-controlled input to trace to a sink.

sink: raw bytes written directly to the stdin of a running shell/REPL process
guard: none: interactWithProcess() (improved-process-tools.ts:388-450) calls terminalManager.sendInputToProcess(pid, input) directly; commandManager.validateCommand() (the blockedCommands check) is called nowhere on this path -- it is only invoked once, from startProcess() (improved-process-tools.ts:120).
why: input is fully caller-controlled (InteractWithProcessArgsSchema: input:string). The documented, primary workflow is start_process('bash'/'python3 -i'/etc.) followed by repeated interact_with_process calls to drive it. Because sendInputToProcess() never calls commandManager.validateCommand(), any command in the server's own blockedCommands list (sudo, dd, mkfs, shutdown, passwd, ...) can be typed into an already-running shell session and executed with zero filtering, completely defeating the operator's blockedCommands configuration that start_process alone enforces.
contract: Send input to a running process and automatically receive the response.

sink: Node process.kill() sends SIGTERM to any OS process id the caller supplies
guard: none: killProcess() only zod-validates that pid is a number; it never checks that the pid belongs to a session/process this server started.
why: pid is fully caller-controlled (KillProcessArgsSchema: pid:number) and is passed straight to process.kill() with no ownership check. This is a real, targeted availability action against an arbitrary process the caller names -- not generic robustness -- and the codebase itself demonstrates the safer pattern is available and simply not used here: the sibling tool force_terminate (improved-process-tools.ts:661-692) is explicitly scoped to terminalManager's own tracked sessions and refuses any pid it did not start ('No active session found for PID'), while kill_process has no equivalent restriction and can terminate any process the OS user running the MCP server can signal.
contract: Terminate a running process by PID. Use with caution as this will forcefully terminate the specified process.

sink: fs.rename() moves the source file/directory onto the resolved destination path
guard: bypassable: isPathAllowed() (filesystem.ts:184-217) authorizes destinationPath by lowercasing both the path and each allowed dir; a destination such as /home/Alice/out.txt (case-different from an existing allowed dir /home/alice) passes the check even though it is a new, case-distinct path that fs.rename will create outside the real allowed directory on a case-sensitive filesystem.

The isUrl branch (readFileFromUrl) is the tool's own advertised URL-fetch feature and uses plain fetch() with no additional twist, so it is not flagged separately.
why: path is caller-controlled (ReadFileArgsSchema). The same lowercase-comparison flaw in isPathAllowed() that makes create_directory/move_file/write_file Tier A also applies to reads, but for read_file the target file must pre-exist with mismatched case relative to the allowed directory, which is a much weaker, state-dependent precondition than the write case.

readProcessOutput reads terminalManager's already-buffered output for a pid by offset/length; it does not execute, open, or interpret any caller-supplied string.

sink: persists allowedDirectories/blockedCommands (or any other CONFIG_FIELD_KEYS entry) to the server's on-disk config, immediately changing the guard every other filesystem/process tool relies on
guard: partial: the key is restricted to a fixed allow-list (isConfigFieldKey/CONFIG_FIELD_DEFINITIONS in config-field-definitions.ts), which prevents arbitrary-key/prototype-pollution issues, but there is no additional confirmation, authorization, or rate-limit before allowedDirectories or blockedCommands is overwritten in one call.
why: set_config_value's own docstring documents the exact risk ("Setting allowedDirectories to an empty array ([]) allows full access to the entire file system") and setConfigValue() (config.ts:158-247) applies no gate beyond zod/key validation before calling configManager.setValue(). A single tool call from the same untrusted context that could feed a prompt-injected instruction to the model can disable the confinement that create_directory/read_file/write_file/etc. depend on, and there is no code-level confirmation step -- only a comment recommending a 'separate chat', which is not enforced.
contract: WARNING: Should be used in a separate chat from file operations and command execution to prevent security issues. IMPORTANT: Setting allowedDirectories to an empty array ([]) allows full access to the entire file system.

sink: commandManager.validateCommand() result gates whether terminalManager spawns the command in a real shell (spawn with shell:true / shell -c, terminal-manager.ts getShellSpawnArgs)
guard: bypassable: extractCommands()/extractBaseCommand() (command-manager.ts:11-227) preserve literal quote characters when splitting on separators (the quote-toggle branches at lines 46-56 append the quote char itself to currentCmd), so for a command like "'sudo' -v" the extracted token is the literal string 'sudo' (with quotes) and path.basename(...).toLowerCase() yields "'sudo'", which never matches a blockedCommands entry of "sudo". The real shell that later executes the command strips the quotes and runs sudo normally, so blockedCommands is bypassed for any blocked command by simply quoting its name (e.g. command: "'sudo' -v" or '"dd" if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sda').
why: command is fully caller-controlled (StartProcessArgsSchema: command:string) and is validated only by commandManager.validateCommand() before being spawned in an actual shell. The blocklist check operates on a token that still contains the caller's quote characters, while the shell that executes the command interprets and strips those quotes, so quoting a blocked command's name (sudo, dd, mkfs, shutdown, passwd, ...) is a concrete, minimal-effort bypass of the operator's blockedCommands guard.
contract: Start a new terminal process with intelligent state detection.

sink: ripgrep is spawned with the resolved rootPath as its search root, and matching file names/contents are returned to the caller
guard: bypassable in principle via the same isPathAllowed() lowercase-comparison flaw (filesystem.ts:184-217), but start_search requires rootPath to already exist (ripgrep errors on a missing directory), so exploitation depends on a pre-existing case-differing directory tree outside the intended allowed dir.
why: path/rootPath is caller-controlled (StartSearchArgsSchema). It is validated once through the same validatePath()/isPathAllowed() call used by the read tools, inheriting the same case-insensitive comparison weakness; because the searched root must already exist, this is a weaker, state-dependent case than the write-side tools.
contract: Unlike regular search tools, this starts a background search process and returns immediately with a session ID.

why: stop_search only stops an in-memory search session by its session id; no path, command, or query is derived from caller input.

sink: handler.write(validPath, content, mode) writes caller-supplied content to the resolved path
